title: Crossing the Red Sea
lead: When there is no way out of a hard place, God can make one.
questions: Which sea in your life are you still only crying out to the Lord about, even though you have already heard Him say: go forward?
What would be your tambourine packed before the miracle: what sign of hope can you get ready before you see it?
Whose faith is running a step behind God’s work, and do you have as much patience with that person as God does?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: A few days after the night of their deliverance, Israel stood at the place where the options ran out: the sea in front, and behind them six hundred chariots of a Pharaoh who had decided he’d made a mistake letting his free labor go. And that was when a voice spoke up, one that would come back again and again on their journey through the wilderness: “Was it because there were no graves in Egypt…?” One look at the pursuit was enough to make slavery seem more sensible than salvation. Fear seemed stronger than gratitude.

The answer came in two commands that sound like a contradiction but actually follow one another. First Moses: “Do not be afraid… The LORD will fight for you; you need only to be still.” Then, right after, God: “Why are you crying out to Me? Tell the Israelites to go forward.” The order to march came before there was a road. First you stop panicking, then you take a step: God opens the sea for people who are walking toward it. The Lord was already sending rescue through the pillar of cloud that moved between the two camps: to Egypt it was darkness, to Israel it was light. Then the sea was split open, and the people crossed on dry ground, “with walls of water on their right and on their left.” When the waters came crashing down, the Egyptians cried out, “The LORD is fighting for them.” It was a confession of faith, made too late.

The chapter ends with a sentence worth reading slowly: “When Israel saw the great power… the people feared the LORD and believed in Him.” They believed after the crossing, not before. That doesn’t mean they had no faith at all until then; Exodus mentions their faith even before the plagues. Here their trust is confirmed after they have seen their rescue. Let’s be patient with people whose faith runs a step behind God’s work; the Lord is. On the far side of the sea, Miriam took out a tambourine, and all the women followed her. Where do tambourines come from in the desert? They had packed them on Passover night, somewhere between the dough and the sandals: luggage ready for a joy no one could see yet. Maybe that is the shortest definition of hope: packing your tambourine before the sea parts.

There was a shorter route from Egypt to Canaan, along the coast. God didn’t choose it, because Egyptian garrisons lined that road, and a people just out of slavery would have turned back to Egypt after the first skirmish. So He led them the long way around, through the wilderness, toward the sea. On a map it looked like a navigational error, and that is exactly how Pharaoh read it: “They are wandering the land in confusion; the wilderness has boxed them in.” Sometimes the road God leads us on looks, from the outside, as if we’ve gotten lost. Sometimes it feels that way from the inside, too. But inside this apparent mistake there was another divine calculation, and the text states it plainly: the Lord knew how much His people could take better than they did, and He didn’t march them to a front they weren’t ready for. A road that spares us a battle beyond our strength rarely gets any credit, because by definition we never see the wars that passed us by.

sections.heading: The Sea Ahead, Egypt Behind
paragraphs: A few days after their liberation, Israel stands at the place where the options run out: water in front, and behind them a cloud of dust over six hundred chariots. Pharaoh has cooled off after that night and decided he made a mistake letting his free labor go. Freedom that hasn’t yet had time to settle can always expect the old life to come after it. And that is when a voice speaks up in Israel, one that will keep coming back all through the wilderness: “Was it because there were no graves in Egypt that you brought us into the wilderness to die?” That one sentence holds the whole psychology of new freedom. Just a week ago they were eating the lamb with their sandals on, ready to go. But now one look at the pursuit is enough to make slavery seem more sensible than salvation: “it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness.” Fear seems stronger than gratitude. Notice, too, who they aim their complaint at. Not at God, who has been leading them in the pillar of cloud, but at Moses, because he is within reach. Panic in a community still works that way: it hits the person standing closest, because it’s harder to pick a fight with the Invisible One.

sections.heading: Two Commands That Sound Like a Contradiction
paragraphs: Moses answers with some of the most beautiful words in the Old Testament: “Do not be afraid. Stand firm and you will see the LORD’s salvation, which He will accomplish for you today… The LORD will fight for you; you need only to be still.” Stand firm, watch, be still. There is an hour in the spiritual life when a person’s only job is not to run. But right after that, God says something to Moses that sounds like the opposite: “Why are you crying out to Me? Tell the Israelites to go forward.” Go forward. Where? The sea is still in front of them. The order to march comes before there is a road. These two commands don’t contradict each other; they follow one another. First you stop panicking, then you take a step. Prayer that endlessly takes the place of moving stops being prayer and becomes a hiding place. God opens the sea for people who are walking toward it.

sections.heading: The Cloud That Was Darkness and Light
paragraphs: Before the water parts, something quiet happens, something easy to miss: “the pillar of cloud also moved from before them and stood behind them, so that it came between the camps of Egypt and Israel.” And the King James Version puts the rest of it this way: “it was a cloud and darkness to them, but it gave light by night to these” (KJV). The same cloud, the same night, two sides. For the oppressors, darkness no one could get through; for Israel, light until morning. The darkness that was chaos on the first page of the Bible is used here by God as a shield for His people. There is a lesson in that for anyone standing in a night they don’t understand: the same night can be the end for some and protection for others, and from inside it you can’t always tell which side of the cloud you’re on.

sections.heading: Waters Split Apart
paragraphs: “Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and all that night the LORD drove back the sea with a strong east wind that turned it into dry land. So the waters were divided.” The Hebrew verb used in that sentence means splitting, the way you split wood or rock. The sea didn’t politely step aside. It was cut open, and all night long the wind dried out the passage, like a worker finishing a road someone else had broken through. “And the Israelites went through the sea on dry ground, with walls of water on their right and on their left.” They walked through the middle of what, that same evening, had looked like their death sentence. And it wasn’t over in a moment: all night, in a darkness lit only by the cloud, families with children, old people, livestock, everyone passed between two walls of water that could have come crashing down on them any second. Leaving slavery, even when it’s a miracle, is often a long march straight through the middle of your own fear. When the Egyptians decided to follow them, their chariots started breaking down: “He caused their chariot wheels to wobble, so that they had difficulty driving. ‘Let us flee from the Israelites,’ said the Egyptians, ‘for the LORD is fighting for them against Egypt!’” Egypt’s last words about the God of Israel were a confession of faith, made too late.

sections.heading: No Road Back
paragraphs: One result of that night rarely gets mentioned. The sea that closed behind Israel buried the pursuit, but it closed something else, too: the road back. Over the next forty years the people would cry out many times that they wanted to go back to Egypt, and once they would even pick themselves a leader for the purpose. But between them and Egypt there was now a sea that no one was going to open a second time. God knew who He was traveling through the wilderness with. If they had been left an open gate, they would have used it the first time they got hungry. There are crossings in life after which God, in His grace, burns the bridge behind us, and what looks like being cut off at the moment of crossing turns out, years later, to have been a rescue. You could still get back to Egypt by land, so the sea didn’t physically close every way back. But it did end Pharaoh’s pursuit, and it became the border between slavery and a new road.

sections.heading: They Believed After the Fact
paragraphs: Chapter 14 ends with a sentence it’s easy to read without surprise: “When Israel saw the great power that the LORD had exercised over the Egyptians, the people feared the LORD and believed in Him and in His servant Moses.” They believed at that moment, after the crossing. That doesn’t mean they had no faith at all before; Exodus mentions the people’s faith even before the plagues. Here their trust is confirmed once again after they have seen their rescue. It’s worth remembering before we judge someone’s faith as late or too dependent on circumstances: God brought through people whose trust still needed strengthening. He led the frightened, the grumbling, the ones looking back over their shoulders at Egypt, and not for a moment did He make their rescue depend on the quality of their faith. There are no heroes of faith in this story. There is a God who makes a road for people like us. And one more thing needs saying: the miracle itself didn’t convert anyone for good. The Egyptians saw the same split sea Israel saw and drew exactly the opposite conclusion: they went into it as a pursuing army. Three days after the victory song, Israel would already be grumbling about water. An eyewitness sees the event, but no witness sees whose hand is behind it; that is decided in the heart, not in the eyes. That is why faith built only on spectacular signs lasts about three days’ march. God knows that, and He gives signs anyway. That is how patient He is with our short memories.

sections.heading: The Same Water
paragraphs: There is a symmetry in this scene that we already know from the story of Noah: the same water that carried the ark buried that old world. It’s similar here. The same walls of water that stood on either side of Israel as they crossed came crashing down on the Egyptians. The sea wasn’t good or bad; God used the same thing for rescue and for judgment. Israel went in at God’s word; Egypt went in on its own initiative, chasing someone else’s freedom. The same act of God can be rescue for some and the end for others, and the difference isn’t in the water.

sections.heading: A Song on the Other Side
paragraphs: Chapter 15 opens with the first song recorded in the Bible: “The LORD is my strength and my song.” And at the end of that song, Miriam steps out with a tambourine, and all the women follow her, dancing. There is a detail in this picture that is moving once you notice it: where do tambourines come from in the desert? The text doesn’t say. Those women, packing in a hurry on Passover night, somewhere between the dough and the sandals, probably took their instruments along. They walked out of slavery with luggage ready for a joy no one could see yet. Maybe that is the shortest definition of hope in this whole story: packing your tambourine before the sea parts. The song itself asks a question Israel would go on repeating in prayer for centuries: “Who among the gods is like You, O LORD?” A week earlier it would have been sung with trembling. Now it comes from the mouths of a people who have crossed the sea on dry ground. And one more detail: Miriam’s song isn’t a solo, it’s a call, “Sing to the LORD,” and the rest of the assembly answers. Someone has to start singing first so the community can find its voice. Maybe that is why God puts people with tambourines in every community.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: This story is for people who have run out of options: an impassable obstacle in front, and behind them a past that won’t let go. Hope here doesn’t mean the problem will turn out smaller than it looked. The sea was exactly as deep as they thought. Hope means that God can find a way where there was none, and that the command “go forward” sometimes comes before the solution shows up. Centuries later, Paul would write that in this passage through the water Israel was, in a sense, baptized: the old life stayed on the other side, and the pursuit was over for good. And one more important thing for us as a community: the people the Almighty brought through that night only believed on the far shore. Let’s be patient with people whose faith runs a step behind God’s work. The Lord is.
